children: Starknet (STRK) extended its rally on Sunday after its parent company, StarkWare, warned that "the quantum threat may be much closer than we think," as the firm behind the network weighs breaking away from Ethereum (ETH) to move faster on security.

The rally came as StarkWare co-founder and CEO Eli Ben-Sasson explained that blockchains needed to become "future-proofed" quickly, because artificial intelligence was advancing fast enough to bring quantum computing's threat to cryptography closer than most people assumed.

“You need better error-correcting codes for qubits, and you need algorithms with fewer qubits. AI is improving each one of these three things, and it is doing so at an ever-greater pace. The recent ECDSA fail project showed how you can drastically reduce the number of qubits needed to basically do discrete log and break ECDSA. The bottom line of all of this is that AI is speeding up the timeline towards breaking Bitcoin and Ethereum signatures with Quantum computers.”
- Eli Ben-Sasson, CEO of StarkWare and co-founder of Zcash
Previosly, the CEO said, quantum threat could become a reality much sooner than we anticipate. A rally has followed ever since.

A Chain That Can't Move

That closing window was what pushed Ben-Sasson to lay out what blockchain needed to survive it. He called for "bunker mode,” and said a future-proofed chain needed three things. These included the right cryptography, the ability to upgrade that cryptography without friction, and in Starknet's case, possibly becoming its own Layer 1.

He pointed to the timeline gap between blockchains, saying that Ethereum was targeting full quantum resistance by the end of 2029. According to him, Starknet could get there by next year, but only if it wasn’t forced to wait on Ethereum first.

Ethereum’s price was relatively flat during the past 24 hours. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around ETH moved to ‘extremely bearish’ from ’ bearish ’, while chatter around it dipped to ‘low‘ from ‘normal’ levels over the past day.
A Test Run On Bitcoin
Starknet also published proof that the idea already works, built on the chain it says is least able to adapt quickly: Bitcoin.

In August, StarkWare researcher Avihu Levy spent a Bitcoin output on mainnet using a method called Quantum-Safe Bitcoin, which locks funds with hash-based cryptography instead of the elliptic-curve keys a quantum computer could eventually break.
The transaction went straight to the mining pool MARA Holdings Inc. (MARA), since Bitcoin's standard software doesn't recognize it. Cost has since dropped from about $320 to around $50.

Starknet was clear that it doesn't make Bitcoin quantum-resistant. The real fix still needs Bitcoin's own developers to approve a software upgrade, which typically takes years. Starknet said this shows how expensive and slow it gets on a chain that can't change its own cryptography.
The market had already reacted once before Sunday’s move. STRK jumped more than 30% on Friday, its biggest single-day gain in over a year.
STRK is up 37% so far this year.
